pages.x: Nader was born around 1688 in Khorasan, in the northeast of Iran, into a poor family of the Turkic Afshar tribe. By the 1720s Persia was falling apart: Afghan rebels had taken the capital, Isfahan, and the Ottomans and Russians were seizing its provinces. Nader, by then a warlord with his own army, offered his sword to the fugitive Safavid heir, Tahmasp.

In 1729 Nader's drilled musketeers and cannon routed the Afghans at Damghan, and again near Isfahan, and Tahmasp entered his ruined capital. Nader chased the Afghans south past Shiraz until their army fell apart. Then he turned west and drove the Ottomans out of western Persia.

Nader deposed Tahmasp in 1732 and ruled for his baby son. After crushing the main Ottoman army in 1735, he called the chiefs and nobles of Persia to a great gathering on the Mughan plain in 1736. As he had arranged, they asked him to become shah. The Safavid dynasty, which had ruled for over two centuries, was over.

Nader then struck east. He took Kandahar after a year-long siege, then Kabul, and in 1738 forced the Khyber Pass into India. On 24 February 1739 at Karnal, north of Delhi, he met the army of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, far larger but slow and badly led, and beat it in about three hours.

Nader entered Delhi as the guest of the beaten emperor. When a rumour spread that he had been killed, people attacked his soldiers. The next morning, 22 March 1739, he sat in a mosque and let his troops loose on the city, until in the afternoon he sheathed his sword and called a halt.
pages.of: people killed in Delhi in one day

pages.x: Nader carried home the treasure of the Mughals: gold, jewels, the jewelled Peacock Throne of Shah Jahan, and a huge diamond, the Koh-i-Noor, the Mountain of Light, a name he is said to have given it.
pages.fx: It was so much that he let Persia off its taxes for three years. The throne was broken up after his death, and the Koh-i-Noor passed from hand to hand until it ended up among the British crown jewels.

pages.x: On his way home Nader crossed the Oxus into Central Asia. The khan of Bukhara gave in without a fight. The khan of Khiva fought, lost and was put to death, and thousands of Persians held as slaves in Khiva were set free. Nader's empire now reached from the Caucasus to the Indus and the Oxus.

The wars went on, and grew harder. In the mountains of Dagestan his army bled in a guerrilla war it could not win. After a shot was fired at him from a forest in 1741, Nader came to suspect his eldest son, Reza Qoli, and had him blinded. He regretted it bitterly, and his cruelty grew.

Taxes to pay for his wars drove province after province into revolt. Nader had officials executed and towers built from the skulls of rebels. In June 1747, at a camp near Quchan, a group of his own officers burst into his tent at night and killed him. Within months his empire had broken apart.

Ahmad Khan, the young commander of Nader's Afghan guard, rode off to Kandahar with his men, and with the Koh-i-Noor. That October a council of Afghan chiefs chose him as their king, Ahmad Shah. His Durrani empire was the beginning of today's Afghanistan.

Nader was one of the last great conquerors of Asia, and for a few years Persia was the strongest power in the Islamic world. But he left little that lasted. Persia fell into years of civil war, and the Mughals never recovered from the sack of Delhi, which opened India to the Marathas and the British.
pts: He saved Persia, then bled it dry
The sack of Delhi broke the Mughals
Afghanistan was born from his empire
